title: My Self Training Claude Code Setup: I Made Claude Code TRAIN ITSELF!
creator: AICodeKing
summary: Applies a Karpathy-style AutoResearch loop to a Claude Code skill: keep the model fixed, edit only one SKILL.md, score each edit against a frozen evaluator, keep or revert. The demo domain is Python bug fixing, not motion graphics, but the method is a direct template for tuning a motion-graphics skill against fixed render checks. Stresses validating the grader first and confirming wins on held-out tasks to avoid overfitting.
what_is_shown: No motion graphics. Terminal sessions running headless Claude Code trials, an evaluator harness, score tables and instruction diffs for a bugfix skill.

techniques.name: Frozen evaluator before optimization
techniques.how: Build the grader first and prove it works: known-broken input must fail, a reviewed good output must pass, tampered outputs (deleted tests, forbidden files) must be rejected; timeouts count as failures.
techniques.quality_lever: A motion skill tuned against an untested checker learns to game it; a validated checker (frame diffs, overlap/contrast/timing checks) makes improvements real.

techniques.name: One-change-per-candidate skill edits
techniques.how: Each candidate revision of the skill file changes a single instruction, visible in the diff and traceable to behavior in transcripts; regressions revert to the previous best.
techniques.quality_lever: Attributes quality gains to specific rules (e.g. a banned-effects line) instead of bundled guesses.

techniques.name: Bare-mode isolated trials
techniques.how: Run trials headless in bare mode, injecting the instruction body with an append-system-prompt-file flag so memory, plugins and CLAUDE.md cannot leak in; fix model, effort, tools, turns and time.
techniques.quality_lever: Makes skill A/B comparisons reproducible.

techniques.name: Held-out confirmation
techniques.how: After search, compare winner vs original on tasks the optimizer never saw, alternating run order under identical limits.
techniques.quality_lever: Prevents a skill overfit to three demo briefs from being adopted.

techniques.name: Hard budget caps
techniques.how: Use max-budget and max-turns flags plus an external timeout and a controller-level spend cap; fix attempt counts in advance.
techniques.quality_lever: Render-heavy motion trials are expensive; caps keep tuning loops affordable.

prompting_patterns: A /autoresearch loop prompt telling the optimizer it may edit only the skill file, against a fixed metric
Success framed as a checkable metric rather than 'make it better'
pipeline: baseline skill + commit -> build & validate frozen evaluator -> baseline trials (3 tasks x 3 attempts) -> 3 single-change candidates -> keep/revert -> held-out comparison -> clean winner diff -> re-test -> adopt
pitfalls: Overfitting to a tiny dev set
Grader that can be edited or fooled
Counting infra errors/timeouts wrongly
Bare mode needs API credentials, not subscription login
Reported dollar costs are estimates; ~48 trials for a small study
Extending attempts until a version looks lucky
evidence: Watch page description with chapters and key takeaways; third-party transcript page (youtubetotranscript) summarized.

title: Every app on Earth is now open source... whether it likes it or not
creator: Fireship
summary: News segment on a developer who reportedly rebuilt several Adobe Creative Cloud apps in Rust with Claude's help and open-sourced them, plus a demo of a reverse-engineering tool used with Ghidra to have a coding agent reimplement a Premiere timeline feature. No motion-graphics authoring workflow is covered; the host found the Premiere-like clone laggy with weak transitions.
what_is_shown: Fireship-style fast-cut commentary; testing of an open-source Premiere-like editor; decompilation demo. No generated motion graphics.
pipeline: binary -> decompile/analyze -> coding agent reimplements feature in Rust (as described; not motion-related)
pitfalls: Cloned editor reportedly laggy with poor transitions
Auto-generated transcript may misspell names (project called Artcraft and FilmCraft inconsistently)
evidence: Watch page description (bot-protected, duration missing) and a third-party auto transcript summary.

title: Anthropic's New Claude NEXT Leak Exposes a MAJOR Breakthrough
creator: AI Revolution
summary: Rumor roundup about an unconfirmed stronger Claude model seen by testers, plus Google's Gemini Enterprise agent. Relevant only because many cited demos are code-drawn animations (a JS-drawn 30-second life story, doodle characters, an anime-style short), and the video correctly notes these are code the model writes, not native video generation. Claims about the model are unverified.
what_is_shown: User-reported demos: frame-by-frame JavaScript animated short, walking doodle with moving shadow, paper-cutout scene, 3D car render, shaded SVG controller, cabin scene with orbiting camera, model-to-model comparison scenes.

techniques.name: Code-drawn hybrid shorts
techniques.how: Motion, effects and transitions are written as code while a few background images and the music are sourced elsewhere.
techniques.quality_lever: Mixing code motion with a small number of crafted assets raises perceived production value beyond pure vector output.

techniques.name: Fixed-scene model comparison
techniques.how: Run the same scene prompt (fish tank, glass cabin) across model versions to compare output quality.
techniques.quality_lever: A standing reference scene set is a cheap regression benchmark for a motion skill.

prompting_patterns: Very short prompt (about four lines) plus long agentic run time (hours) reported for a 30s film
pipeline: short prompt -> long agentic code-writing session -> code-rendered animation (+ external music/backgrounds)
pitfalls: Hype: code visuals replacing video generators is overstated
Model identity unverified; check model ID via /model or the models API
evidence: Watch page description (bot-protected) and third-party transcript summary; demos are second-hand reports, not inspected.

title: Turn Claude Into a Motion Design GENIUS
creator: Duncan Rogoff | Learn Claude Code
summary: A five-step method for getting premium promo videos from Claude instead of generic output: gather strong references (via prompt-motion.com), have Claude analyze them, distill a design-system file, approve one still per scene type before animating, then give concrete designer-style feedback that gets written back into the design system. The creator says the biggest gain came from showing references, not from a cleverer prompt.
what_is_shown: Branded promo films for a whiskey site and the creator's dark/green brand; a dot-based visual motif; a scrapped watch promo; before/after comparison of one-line vs detailed prompts.

techniques.name: Reference-first prompting
techniques.how: Pick reference videos whose exact prompts are published and reuse the detailed ones as a base, swapping in your own brand copy and imagery.
techniques.quality_lever: Detailed prompts transfer style; one-liners leave gaps Claude fills with generic choices and invented facts.

techniques.name: Reference teardown with borrow/avoid lists
techniques.how: Ask Claude to break each reference into color, type, layout, motion and pacing, then merge into one summary with moves to borrow and things to exclude for this brand.
techniques.quality_lever: Keeps the result inspired-by rather than a copy, and blocks off-brand carryover (e.g. white scenes).

techniques.name: Design-system file as persistent rules
techniques.how: Write one file of look-and-motion rules from the site's colors/fonts plus borrowed motion and house rules such as every scene fills the frame and nothing overlaps.
techniques.quality_lever: Stops drift across scenes and generations; a rule fixed once stays fixed.

techniques.name: Stills gate before animation
techniques.how: Request one poster-like still per scene type, review and fix them, and only then animate.
techniques.quality_lever: Catches layout bugs (duplicate logo, dark-on-dark invisible logo) before 11-20 minute render cycles.

techniques.name: Designer-style feedback loop
techniques.how: Give notes that name a problem and a fix, include feel-level direction (one continuous camera move), say what to keep, revise one round at a time, and write each fix into the design system.
techniques.quality_lever: Converts taste into durable constraints and preserves what works.

techniques.name: Fix the right layer
techniques.how: When output feels neither premium nor on-brief, change subject or references rather than polishing.
techniques.quality_lever: Avoids sunk-cost iteration on a fundamentally weak direction.

prompting_patterns: Paste a detailed published reference prompt and substitute brand inputs
Analyze these references: colors, typography, layout, motion, pacing; output borrow list + leave-out list
Create a design system file covering how everything looks and moves
Give me one still frame per scene type before any video
pipeline: find references -> Claude studies them (borrow/avoid) -> design system file -> stills per scene type -> approve -> animate/render -> designer review rounds -> write fixes back to design system
pitfalls: Short prompts produce invented content such as fake statistics
Copying references too closely
Skipping the leave-out list
No design system causes drift
Rendering before approving stills wastes long render cycles
Vague feedback
Polishing a fundamentally wrong concept
evidence: Watch page description with chapters and five steps; third-party transcript summary covering each step. Free prompt guide link was truncated and not read.

title: Prompt Motion
creator: @p4nthera_ (curator)
summary: A curated gallery of roughly 233 motion videos made with Claude Opus 5.5, each linked to the prompt or skill that produced it, with category filters, a prompt customizer, templates and a data-driven blog. The blog mines the gallery: long prompts that settle decisions (single concept, banned list, beat grid, build method, self-review) outperform the dominant 26-word one-liners, and it compares renderers (plain HTML + Playwright, Remotion, HyperFrames, Three.js). Likes are acknowledged as a noisy quality signal.
what_is_shown: Gallery categories: kinetic type, product UI, music, shapes, particles, charts, diagrams, characters, photos, phone, code. Launch videos and showreels dominate. Templates: a 15s showreel brief rewrite and a real-time three.js template.

techniques.name: Deterministic seek(t) build
techniques.how: One HTML file where every visual is computed from time in a seek function; no CSS transitions, timers, Math.random or carried state; headless browser seeks each frame and ffmpeg encodes.
techniques.quality_lever: Frame-exact, reproducible renders that cannot drop frames or drift from audio.

techniques.name: Subframe motion blur
techniques.how: Render about three subframes per output frame at 60fps and blend them with ffmpeg's tmix; blur scales with speed.
techniques.quality_lever: Removes the strobing, too-clean look of code animation on fast moves.

techniques.name: Banned-effects line with paired replacements
techniques.how: One line of five to nine bans (glows, particle bursts, lens flares, crossfades, bouncy easing, corner text, generic gradients, camera shake, RGB split, long holds) ending with 'anything template-like', each paired with an alternative; grow it by adding whatever unrequested effect showed up in the last run.
techniques.quality_lever: Blocks Claude's default AI-looking moves, the most cited tell.

techniques.name: Single concept with connected transitions
techniques.how: Name one concept up front; every shot grows out of the previous one through one element morphing (circle to square to pill) or a recurring element instead of cuts or fades.
techniques.quality_lever: Reads as designed continuity rather than a slideshow of effects.

techniques.name: Beat-grid timing
techniques.how: State tempo and bar count (e.g. 120 BPM, change on every beat, hook in bar one, strongest moment in the last full bar, end title in the final half bar); optionally detect beats in real audio with numpy.
techniques.quality_lever: Beat-matched changes were the clearest difference between launch films and feature slideshows.

techniques.name: Constrained springs and easing
techniques.how: Use closed-form springs with very small overshoot plus exponential easing; drive graphs from the same spring function that moves the object.
techniques.quality_lever: Lively but not cartoonish; synchronized elements stay locked together.

techniques.name: Beat map + stills, then per-beat frame review
techniques.how: Ask for inputs first, deliver a beat-by-beat storyboard and a few key stills, then render one frame per beat to check clutter, overlaps, timing and readability before the full export.
techniques.quality_lever: Cheap visual QA gate that catches overlapping text and empty frames.

techniques.name: Typography and palette constraints
techniques.how: One typeface (Geist/Inter or a bold display face), at most three colors plus black and white, warm off-white or near-black ground with one consistent accent; separate in/out timing for text; per-letter animation for word morphs.
techniques.quality_lever: Restraint reads as premium; separate timing prevents letter collisions.

techniques.name: Seamless loop closure
techniques.how: Match cursor position, speed, dots and type between the last and first frames.
techniques.quality_lever: Avoids a visible stutter on looping social clips.

techniques.name: Code-generated soundtrack
techniques.how: Write audio with the Web Audio API (kick per beat, riser into the final bar, hits on scene changes), render to WAV and mux with the video.
techniques.quality_lever: Sound locked to visual beats without external assets.

techniques.name: Process-shaped explainers
techniques.how: Give the explainer a start-to-finish sequence (empty glass to finished drink with labeled ingredients, or a request moving through a system) or an explicit scene list; budget about five seconds per idea; name audience, narration method and require fact-checking.
techniques.quality_lever: Structure fixed before visuals prevents generic topic montages and invented numbers.

techniques.name: Launch-film inputs block
techniques.how: Collect product name, one-line promise, three to five ordered UI moments, hex colors, one font, light/dark mode, format (e.g. 9:16 pixel size), length, tempo, avoid list and ending (logo/URL/line) before building.
techniques.quality_lever: Makes the prompt reusable and keeps the product as the subject rather than a backdrop.

prompting_patterns: Long briefs (>100 words) that settle duration, tempo/bars, beat events, palette, type, avoid list, build method and review step
Name the renderer explicitly so runs are reproducible
Ask for inputs first, then a beat map and stills, then build without further questions
Recommend Opus 5.5 at max effort for the showreel rewrite (max effort alone did not fix one-liner variance)
Templates expose every likely-changed part as a field
pipeline: inputs block -> single concept + beat map -> key stills -> seek(t) HTML build (or Remotion/HyperFrames) -> per-beat frame review -> Playwright 60fps capture with subframes -> ffmpeg tmix blur + encode -> Web Audio WAV mux -> MP4
pitfalls: One-liner prompts produce wildly variable results (same 26-word prompt: 0 to ~17k likes, median 5)
Unnamed renderer means Claude picks a different stack each run
will-change on camera-scaled elements blurs text
Text in morphing containers overlaps without its own enter/exit timing
Mismatched first/last frames stutter on loop
Math.random breaks reproducibility
Three.js adds cost for flat design
Remotion licensing may require a paid license for some companies
Likes are a weak quality proxy; small samples
Explainer prompts never asked for fact-checking
evidence: Fetched home page, blog index, four blog posts (look-less-AI, Remotion vs HyperFrames, 230-prompt analysis, explainer prompts, launch prompts) and templates page plus showreel template. Individual gallery prompts not read.

title: This ONE Claude Skill Helps You Think Clearer Than 99% of People
creator: Nate Herk | AI Automation
summary: Shows a Claude Code skill where a chair session runs seven persona sub-agents through opening positions with scores, cross-examination (including forced devil's-advocate assignments) and a final vote, producing a scored, replayable verdict and PDF. It is a business-decision tool, not motion graphics; the transferable piece is the multi-critic review structure that could judge storyboards or stills.
what_is_shown: A live visual debate UI for the advisor council, round-by-round reasoning, a scored verdict and a PDF export. No motion graphics.

techniques.name: Chair + specialist critic sub-agents
techniques.how: A main session sets the question per round and routes debate among persona sub-agents, each backed by a folder of decision rules, frameworks and voice notes.
techniques.quality_lever: Distinct critic lenses (e.g. typographer, motion director, brand) give sharper review of a storyboard than one generic self-review.

techniques.name: Score, cross-examine, vote
techniques.how: Round one: each critic scores options out of 10; round two: critics respond to each other, some assigned to argue against their preference; round three: final vote and chair verdict with conditions.
techniques.quality_lever: Counters agreeable self-critique.

techniques.name: Relevance-weighted panel
techniques.how: Weight critics by relevance and invoke only the most relevant subset per question.
techniques.quality_lever: Keeps review cost down.

prompting_patterns: State the decision, two or three options, real numbers, limits, success criteria, and the option you lean toward so the panel can challenge it
pipeline: question brief -> opening scored positions -> cross-examination -> final vote -> verdict + PDF
pitfalls: Accepting the verdict without understanding it
Agent teams cost more than sub-agents without better answers
No iterative revision of a work product; dissent resolved only by the chair
evidence: Watch page description with chapters; third-party transcript summary.

title: Obsidian Excalidraw CLI: GPT-6 Luna vs 6.1 Sol (Full Workflow & Benchmark)
creator: Zsolt's Visual Personal Knowledge Management
summary: Demonstrates a new Obsidian Excalidraw CLI plus agent skill repo that lets coding agents build native, editable Excalidraw drawings, benchmarked by having a cheap and an expensive model recreate a raster infographic as vectors. The key mechanic is a render-export-look-compare loop: the agent exports a PNG, views it against the target, and edits. Static diagrams, not animation, but the vision loop and reusable-object approach transfer directly to SVG motion work.
what_is_shown: Editable Excalidraw recreation of an AI infographic (robot, cog, folder, lightbulb, magnifier) iterating over versions; side-by-side model comparison; saving a vector robot to the stencil library.

techniques.name: Render-and-look vision loop
techniques.how: Agent builds the drawing, exports a PNG, inspects it against the reference image, then edits and repeats.
techniques.quality_lever: Lets the model catch missing text, misplaced labels and broken shapes it cannot see from source alone; the same loop applies to rendered motion stills.

techniques.name: Reusable vector objects
techniques.how: The stronger model built recurring elements (robot, cog, logo) as reusable objects and refined them across iterations; finished objects saved to a stencil library.
techniques.quality_lever: A reusable asset library improves consistency and speeds later pieces.

techniques.name: Sandbox workspace for agents
techniques.how: Give the agent a separate vault with copied reference images to iterate in.
techniques.quality_lever: Safe free iteration without polluting real projects.

techniques.name: Skill repo pointer prompt
techniques.how: Short prompt pointing the agent at the CLI skill repository plus the target image.
techniques.quality_lever: Tool knowledge lives in the skill, keeping the prompt minimal.

prompting_patterns: Point the agent at the skill repository and ask it to recreate the attached image as native editable elements
pipeline: enable CLI -> sandbox vault + reference image -> agent reads skill repo -> build drawing -> export PNG -> compare -> iterate -> editable vectors -> save to library
pitfalls: Early iterations omitted text entirely
Objects disappeared between iterations
Wrong text placement and line details mid-run
Cheap model fast but weak on detail; strong model ~16 min and ~10x cost
evidence: Watch page description with setup steps, repos and chapters; third-party transcript summary. Skill repo contents not read.

title: The S TIER Claude Code Mods
creator: Ray Amjad
summary: Tour of Claude Code plugins ('mods') that share one pattern: after each turn a cheap check (Haiku call or a classifier) decides if side work is worth doing, then forks the conversation on the same prompt cache to do it while the main session continues. Mods include memory updating, a diagram side pane, a periodic memory 'dream' pass, a swarm monitor, decision trees, a cache clock, a classifier-based skill router, a secret box and a vague-prompt bouncer. No animation; relevance is in harness patterns.
what_is_shown: Side panes: session-decision diagrams with a shape key, pinned Mermaid diagrams, decision-tree map view, skill-probability display, swarm stats for ~100 parallel agents. No motion graphics.

techniques.name: Cheap per-turn gate then forked side task
techniques.how: A small model or classifier inspects each turn and, when warranted, forks the session (sharing prompt cache) to run a side job such as updating memory or a diagram.
techniques.quality_lever: Lets a motion skill run QA or design-system updates in parallel without bloating the main context.

techniques.name: Classifier skill router
techniques.how: Classify the typed prompt to suggest or load only the top few relevant skills, showing probabilities.
techniques.quality_lever: Keeps large motion reference skills out of context until needed.

techniques.name: Prompt bouncer
techniques.how: A Haiku check rejects vague prompts before the main agent runs, suggesting glossary terms.
techniques.quality_lever: Directly addresses one-liner briefs that produce generic motion output.

techniques.name: Visual shape key for diagrams
techniques.how: Fixed semantics per shape (square = changed file, rounded = new component, double border = step).
techniques.quality_lever: Consistent visual grammar makes generated diagrams readable.

prompting_patterns: Create mods by describing desired behavior in plain language via /plugin, then reload plugins
pipeline: turn ends -> cheap classifier gate -> fork on shared cache -> side task -> side pane update
pitfalls: Large swarms are expensive (~$180/hour shown)
Memory mod triggered manually in demo though meant to be automatic
Prompt cache windows are short (about 5 minutes for subagents)
evidence: Watch page description with chapters and repo link (github.com/ray-amjad/claude-code-mods, not read); third-party transcript summary.
